title: Neutral Noise-and-Flight Monitors for Drone Hubs
one_liner: Independent noise and flight-log monitoring that gives cities and neighbors a referee for drone-delivery hub permits, and gives operators and retail hosts approvable evidence.
customer: Drone-delivery operators and the retailers hosting hubs at store sites, paying to win and keep permits. City planning departments and neighborhood groups are the audience.
problem: Cities cannot regulate flight paths but can zone launch hubs. Northglenn requires a special-use permit, a 200 ft residential buffer and 65 dB at the property line. Wing and Walmart target 270+ sites by 2027 and Lowe's launched on Sep 28, 2026, so each site needs a hearing. Neighbors distrust operator-supplied noise data, cities lack staff and gear to check 65 dB, and a $5k-$15k consultant noise study is one-off and stale on day one.
solution: A permit-ready package. Before the application, a 7-day baseline at the property lines with calibrated low-cost acoustic sensors. After launch, continuous monitoring, tamper-evident logs, a public dashboard and alerts, matched to operator flight logs to attribute each event. An annual certification report cities can write into conditions of approval. Complaint triage: 'was a drone there at 3:14 pm? yes, 62 dB, within limit.'
why_now: The retail-scale rollout (Walmart/Wing 270+ sites, Lowe's/Wing/DoorDash launch on Sep 28, 2026, Zipline past 2M deliveries) is hitting local ground rules. Amazon paused after an Oct 2025 crane collision, so safety and trust are sensitive. Cities are drafting rules now.
revenue_model: $1,500 baseline and report per site. $300-$600/mo per site for monitoring, dashboard and certification. Optional city-charged permit fee. The city chooses the vendor, and raw data is public to protect neutrality.
non_obvious_insight: Local permitting, not the FAA, is the binding constraint on drone-delivery rollout. The currency of permits is neighbor trust, so a neutral measurement with a public dashboard is worth more than a better noise model. The party both sides accept as referee wins, and the fee is paid by whoever needs approval. Conflict-of-interest guards are the product: public raw data, no success fees, a firewall from operators.
first_30_days: Buy 10 sensors and calibrate them. Pick 3 cities with active hub hearings. Offer a free baseline for one live application at a store site. Get a city planner to reference the method in conditions of approval. Sign the first paid contract with a retail host or operator. Aim for 15-30 monitored sites by month 6.

title: Business Identity Watch: LifeLock for LLCs
one_liner: Continuous monitoring of the state filings, liens and listings that define a small business, with a fast response kit when someone hijacks them.
customer: Owners of LLCs and sole proprietorships, reached through community banks, insurance agents, CPAs and registered-agent companies.
problem: Formation is cheap and online, and US domestic companies no longer file beneficial-ownership reports (FinCEN's final rule, August 2026). Census restated its formation series and excluded internet-sales-linked applications from some series, which suggests formation counts are polluted by non-real businesses (inference). Fraudsters can file fake officer or agent changes, register lookalike LLCs and domains, hijack listings and file bogus liens. Owners find out when a collections letter arrives.
solution: Monitor Secretary of State filings across states with open bulk feeds, UCC indexes, lookalike entity names and domains, and Google Business Profile edits. Alert the owner and provide pre-drafted correction filings, fraud affidavits, a registered-agent switch, and a bank notification letter.
why_now: There is no federal ownership registry to lean on, formation is cheap, and AI makes synthetic-identity and lookalike-business fraud cheaper to run.
revenue_model: $9-19 per entity per month, a $299 incident-response fee, and bulk banking deals at about $2 per entity per month.
non_obvious_insight: The state filing is the root of trust for a small business, and nobody watches it. Identity-theft companies watch people, not entities, and a bank that already knows the business is the natural distributor.
first_30_days: Pick five states with open bulk filing data and build change alerts. Pilot with 200 LLCs through one community bank or bookkeeper. Track fraud events detected and time to resolve.

title: 24/7 named-filer retainer for CRA reporting
one_liner: A follow-the-sun 'fractional PSIRT' that pre-registers, drills and files CRA Article 14 vulnerability reports on the ENISA portal for small connected-device makers.
customer: EU and non-EU manufacturers of connected products with roughly 5-250 staff and no 24/7 security team. Examples are smart-home, IP camera, e-bike and e-scooter electronics, EV charger, industrial IoT gateway, 3D printer and consumer robotics makers. Their CEO or head of product pays.
problem: Since 11 Sept 2026, manufacturers must send an early warning within 24 hours of becoming aware of an actively exploited vulnerability, a fuller notice within 72 hours, and a final report later. This covers products already on the market, including 2019 models. Fines reach EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover. The ENISA portal has no API at launch and needs 39 manual fields. Filers must be named individuals with EU Login and MFA. Picking the wrong coordinator CSIRT can invalidate a filing. The platform's 72-hour counter can show a compliant filing as overdue. Emailing a national CSIRT does not count. Small makers have no one awake on a Sunday who knows any of this.
solution: Sell a monthly retainer with four parts. (1) A pre-flight setup: named EU Login accounts, a documented coordinator-CSIRT choice, a product-to-Member-State map and the required vulnerability contact. (2) A one-page intake form and an 'awareness decision log' that keeps independent 24h/72h/14-day clocks and a defensible record of when the manufacturer became aware. (3) A rotating on-call engineer, holding one of the up-to-20 secondary filer seats under the manufacturer's written designation, who drafts and pastes the 39-field early warning within hours. (4) Twice-yearly tabletop drills that produce an audit-ready evidence file. The manufacturer stays legally responsible. We supply speed and process, not scanners.
why_now: Article 14 became binding on 11 Sept 2026 and the single reporting platform went live the same day. Registration guidance only started rolling out on 31 July. No CRA harmonised standard was in the Official Journal as of late August, and notified-body capacity is a 'best-efforts' December 2026 target. Small makers therefore have no standards shortcut and must run the reporting process by hand.
revenue_model: Setup fee of EUR 1,000-1,500. Retainer of EUR 250-600 per month by product count. Incident filing package of EUR 2-4k per event. Drill add-on of EUR 800. Later, referral or bundle deals with cyber insurers, notified-body consultants and contract manufacturers.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource is a named human with a valid account, awake at 3am, making the 'awareness' judgment call. Scanner vendors are everywhere, but nobody sells the person and the drill. Evidence: the ENISA portal guide says 'Automate the preparation, not the filing' and lists no API, 39 fields, named-person accounts, the wrong-CSIRT risk and the misaligned 72h counter (https://craevidence.com/cra-compliance/enisa-srp-onboarding). An ENISA survey found 20% of SMEs were unsure the CRA even applied to them (https://www.techtarget.com/cybersecurity/feature/EU-Cyber-Resilience-Act-reporting-What-CISOs-need-to-know). Greenbone's readiness review found the platform still in testing two weeks before go-live and no standards published (https://www.greenbone.net/en/blog/cra-article-14-readiness-status/). ENISA launch note: https://www.enisa.europa.eu/news/the-cra-single-reporting-platform-is-launched.
first_30_days: Turn the public ENISA and Commission material into a free 'SRP pre-flight' checklist and a 24h/72h clock template, and publish both. Recruit 4-6 freelance product-security engineers across EU, US and Asia time zones for a rotation. Cold-message about 300 product-security, CE-compliance and CTO contacts at hardware makers (RED and CE registries, hardware crowdfunding lists). Offer 5 founding pilots at EUR 99 per month plus a free first drill. Book a tabletop drill with each pilot and convert the drill output into the case study.

title: Guard-Shack Handshake: Stopping Fictitious Pickups at the Gate
one_liner: A free, no-login gate tool for shipper guard shacks that shows the pre-enrolled driver, truck, plate and a one-time PIN, paid for per protected load by brokers and cargo insurers.
customer: Brokers moving high-theft commodities (electronics, copper and other metals, consumer goods, food and beverage) and their cargo and contingent-cargo insurers pay. Shippers get the guard tool free, which is what drives adoption.
problem: CargoNet estimates H1 2026 cargo theft losses above $359M, with Q2 2026 losses of $304.6M (more than double Q2 2025) even though incidents fell, driven by high-value metals and technology. Criminals now compromise legitimate carrier accounts, internet-based phone systems, email and compliance-platform credentials, so the email domain, callback number and vetting badge can all be authentic-looking. Meanwhile at the physical gate a guard checks a load number and a BOL, as in 1995. The load number is a password that the broker has already emailed to dozens of carriers.
solution: At tender, the broker's rate-con flow triggers a driver self-enrollment via SMS link: selfie, CDL photo, truck and trailer plate photos. The system checks how recently the carrier's public contact info changed and whether the enrolling number matches prior loads. The shipper's shipping desk and guard get a web link (no app, no integration) showing the expected driver photo, plate and USDOT number. The driver must speak a PIN issued only through the enrollment. The guard taps match or mismatch and snaps an arrival photo, and any mismatch alerts the broker and shipper instantly. The receiver gets the same flow at delivery. Aggregated data goes to insurers.
why_now: The 2026 CargoNet reports describe impersonation-based theft as systematic and scalable, with credential and phone-system compromise defeating digital-only checks. Montgomery (May 2026) raised broker liability, and insurers are now asking brokers for controls. The Jan 2026 FMCSA rule means a broker who pays a big theft claim can drop below the bond threshold and face suspension.
revenue_model: $2-$5 per protected load charged to brokers, plus an insurer revenue share or bounty for verified low-loss books. Later, sell a 'verified pickup' certificate to cargo insurers in exchange for lower deductibles.
non_obvious_insight: The thief needs two things, a load number and a plausible carrier identity, and the broker hands out both freely. Nobody has redesigned the 30-second guard-shack transaction because shippers feel the cargo is no longer theirs once the BOL is signed, so the party that eats the loss (broker or insurer) has to fund a free tool for the party that controls the gate. The best fraud tell is not the carrier's score but the age of its contact info: hijacked carriers show new phones and emails days before booking. Brokers whisper this in fraud groups but no product sells it.
first_30_days: Sign 3 brokers hauling metals or electronics and pick 5 recurring shipper docks. Build a web-only MVP (SMS enrollment plus guard view) and run the PINs manually. Pilot 100 loads, measuring driver friction (target under 90 seconds) and catch rate with seeded red-team tests. Get one cargo insurer or MGA to review the pilot data for a premium credit.

title: Loss-Curve Intelligence for Autonomous Trucking Insurance
one_liner: A benchmark and risk-scoring workbench that helps insurers, brokers and carriers price driverless-truck coverage using evidence instead of 'unknown'.
customer: Specialty insurers and reinsurers, MGAs, brokers, and large trucking carriers. AV operators such as Aurora, Kodiak, Bot Auto and Gatik also buy, to lower their premiums.
problem: Insurers price AV trucks 'slightly above' human drivers purely because of the unknown, with premiums expected to fall 15-25% a year. Werner's CIO says 'we have a gap' on pricing. Nobody has normalized exposure data by operating domain.
solution: Ingest public crash reports (NHTSA Standing General Order and state reports), published safety cases and operator-contributed telemetry. Build frequency and severity priors by operating design domain (lane type, speed, weather, time of day) and deliver a quarterly benchmark plus a route and lane risk-scoring API. Later, underwrite as an MGA.
why_now: Aurora exits 2026 with about 200 driverless trucks and 500k+ driverless miles, the first real exposure data, and targets 30,000 trucks by 2030. Insurers must reprice yearly and need evidence to justify each step down.
revenue_model: $75-250k a year in subscriptions from insurers and reinsurers, per-policy data fees, and MGA commission (10-15% of premium) once loss data supports it.
non_obvious_insight: The problem is not too few miles but the lack of a standard exposure unit. Whoever defines miles by operating domain as the accepted denominator becomes the FICO of autonomy, and operators will share data because it lowers their premiums.
first_30_days: Build an ODD-normalized frequency table from public NHTSA data. Interview 15 trucking and AV underwriters, send a free 'AV vs human benchmark' brief to 3 brokers, and close one $30k paid pilot with an MGA.

title: Auracast Hearing Access for Churches and Senior Centers
one_liner: Turnkey Bluetooth Auracast broadcast installs that let people with hearing loss hear services, meetings and group activities directly in their own hearing aids and earbuds.
customer: Houses of worship, senior centers, libraries, community halls and municipal meeting rooms, paying $1.5-6k for install plus $50-150 a month managed service.
problem: Hearing loss is a leading modifiable dementia risk and a quiet driver of withdrawal: people stop going to services, dinners and meetings because they cannot follow. Fewer than one in three adults who could benefit use hearing aids. Legacy hearing loops are costly and often fail unnoticed, and FM systems require borrowing clunky receivers. Venues with amplified sound face ADA assistive-listening obligations that many ignore.
solution: Pre-configured Auracast transmitters (line-in or audio-over-IP) installed in a day, with QR signage ('join the broadcast'), usher training, room-level coverage checks and a remote-monitoring dashboard so it keeps working. Multi-channel support allows a second-language stream (English and Spanish) from the same room.
why_now: Auracast (LE Audio broadcast) is shipping in current hearing aids, phones and earbuds. OTC hearing aids (2022) and AirPods Pro hearing-aid features (Sep-Oct 2024) expanded the user base. Loneliness is now a WHO-measured metric, and venues want visible ways to include older attendees.
revenue_model: Install fee plus recurring managed-service subscription. Referral fees from audiologists and hearing-aid manufacturers seeking demand generation.
non_obvious_insight: The hidden loneliness intervention is upstream of any program: tens of millions of people with hearing loss quietly stop attending. Fixing the room is cheaper than fixing the person, and Auracast collapses the cost of doing it.
first_30_days: Buy three transmitters (about $300-600 each). Install free in three churches or senior centers in one metro with an audiologist partner, capture attendance and testimonials, then sell ten installs at about $2.5k through denominational newsletters and audiologist referrals.

title: Pet Evacuation Capacity Options
one_liner: An annual small-fee option that reserves boarding capacity near you and pays for it automatically when an official evacuation order hits your address.
customer: Pet-owning households in wildfire, hurricane and flood zones, especially those on FAIR plans or recently nonrenewed. Homeowner insurers, brokers and HOAs are second buyers as a retention perk. Boarding kennels, vet clinics and pet-friendly hotels sell the reserved capacity.
problem: Pets are a leading reason people delay or refuse evacuation. In an evacuation the scarce resource is capacity, not money: pet-friendly shelters fill within hours and boarding facilities book out. Homeowners facing record nonrenewals have no cheap product to show insurers are still doing something for them, and kennels' unused capacity is perishable inventory.
solution: Sell an annual $49-79 option: reserved boarding slots (up to 14 days at a pre-agreed rate) at a vetted network within a 2-hour drive. It is triggered automatically when an official evacuation warning polygon covers the owner's address. Vaccination records are pre-verified so facilities accept the pet immediately. Facilities earn a retainer for reserving capacity plus a surge rate when exercised, paid instantly. Launch as a prepaid service reservation and convert to a parametric insurance structure through an MGA later.
why_now: Homeowner nonrenewals set records, California passed three claims and nonrenewal bills on Sept 3, and FAIR plans are growing. Reinsurance is softening with record cat-bond issuance, so parametric capacity is cheap. Instant payment rails exist, and late September is the run-up to peak fire and hurricane exposure.
revenue_model: Annual option premium, B2B2C fees of $10-20 per policy from insurers, brokers or HOAs, and a margin on surge-rate exercises.
non_obvious_insight: Sell a call option on capacity, not an insurance payout. In a crisis the value is in a guaranteed place to put the animal, and kennels would rather sell perishable capacity in advance than hope for demand. Parametric triggers make the whole thing automatic, which insurers love.
first_30_days: Pick one wildfire county. Sign 8 boarding facilities on a small retainer and pre-sell 300 households through fire-safe councils and HOAs. Build the trigger from public evacuation-zone feeds and run reservations manually the first season.

title: Metering Unmetered Wells From Orbit
one_liner: Estimate monthly pumping for every unmetered irrigation well by fusing radar subsidence, satellite crop water use and electricity data, and sell it to groundwater regulators.
customer: Groundwater sustainability agencies (about 140 in California), Texas groundwater conservation districts, Kansas management districts and Arizona active management areas, plus ag lenders, farmland funds and data-center developers relying on groundwater. Agencies pay annual fees.
problem: Most irrigation wells are unmetered, so regulators cannot enforce pumping limits or fees. Broad drought and Colorado River cuts push more pumping onto aquifers, and data centers in rule-of-capture states draw groundwater with little oversight.
solution: Fuse three signals: InSAR ground deformation (seasonal elastic movement tracks aquifer drawdown), ET-based irrigation demand minus effective precipitation, and pump electricity records from cooperating utilities. Calibrate against the wells that are metered and output pumping estimates with uncertainty per parcel and month. Deliver an evidence report agencies can use in fee and compliance programs.
why_now: The NASA-ISRO NISAR radar satellite launched in mid-2025 and its L-band data is open. ET datasets have matured. California's groundwater deadlines and the Texas audit push make measurement urgent.
revenue_model: $30-200k/yr per agency or basin, plus per-report fees to lenders and developers.
non_obvious_insight: Regulators do not need perfect meters, only defensible estimates calibrated against a sample of real ones, which is far cheaper than metering every well. The gap is that ET-only estimates cannot see storage change, and InSAR can.
first_30_days: Pick one critical-overdraft basin or Texas district with a metering plan. Reprocess two years of free Sentinel-1 InSAR, compare with the known meters, and publish a validation memo. Pitch three agencies on a 60-day paid pilot.

title: Data Act Access-Request Desk for Independent Repairers
one_liner: A clearinghouse that files, tracks and escalates EU Data Act data-access requests to connected-product makers on behalf of independent garages, installers and fleet operators.
customer: Independent repair-shop networks, heat-pump and solar installers, agricultural-machinery service firms and small fleet operators (10-500 vehicles or machines) in the EU, plus their trade associations.
problem: Connected products must give users direct data access by design from 12 Sep 2026, and users can direct sharing to third parties. Every manufacturer will build its own portal, format and terms, and has every incentive to slow-walk independents. The EU repair directive transposition deadline (31 Jul 2026) also just passed. Small firms know wrenches, not statutory request letters or how to reach a national competent authority.
solution: A standardized request generator, a directory of each manufacturer's access method, a tracker with statutory-timeline reminders, normalization of the most-wanted data (fault codes, usage, battery health) and an escalation pack for the national authority. Launch with five manufacturers in two product categories.
why_now: The Data Act design obligation date was 12 Sep 2026, the repair directive deadline was 31 Jul 2026 and the EU repair platform is due 1 Jan 2028. Independents just received rights with no plumbing.
revenue_model: $49-149/month per shop, $5-20 per vehicle or machine per year for fleets, association licenses, and paid negotiation of bulk access terms.
non_obvious_insight: Compliance startups sell to the obligated party. The Data Act creates a beneficiary class that is fragmented and unsophisticated about law. The AirHelp pattern applies: rights that are costly to file individually but cheap to file collectively.
first_30_days: Sign two trade associations (independent aftermarket or agricultural repair). Send 20 manual requests across five OEMs and log response times, then publish an 'OEM Data Act responsiveness scorecard' to earn press and members. Charge $99/month.

title: Regulatory Slip Desk for Compliance Budget Decisions
one_liner: A probability-weighted deadline desk that tells compliance heads which rules will probably slip, which will not, and which controls are worth building now regardless.
customer: GCs, heads of compliance and CFOs at companies with $200M-$20B revenue facing many regimes at once (EU AI Act, CBAM, CRA, CSRD, US state privacy and AI laws). Secondary buyers are compliance-software vendors timing their sales and investors betting on delay.
problem: Deadlines have become unreliable. AI Act high-risk duties moved to 2 Dec 2027 (Annex III) and 2 Aug 2028 (Annex I) per the tracker (the Omnibus status is unverified), CSRD waves 2 and 3 slipped to 2028, while CBAM and CRA reporting did not move. Teams either overspend on rules that later slip or get blindsided by rules that hold. Law-firm alerts explain what a rule says, not whether it will arrive on time.
solution: A subscription tracker of about 100 obligations, each with the hard date, a written probability of further slip or scope cut with reasons (trilogue calendar, standards readiness, member-state transposition, litigation), and a split between 'no-regret controls' that satisfy several regimes (inventories, logging, supplier data) and 'wait for clarity' items. Trigger alerts ('if standard X is not cited by date Y, slip probability rises'). A public scored track record of every past forecast, plus a quarterly board memo.
why_now: 2025-26 was the year of delays and unwinds: the Digital Omnibus reshuffled AI Act dates, CSRD got stop-the-clock, and several US rules were dropped or vacated (background, verify). Buyers have now been burned in both directions.
revenue_model: $12-40k/year per enterprise seat pack, a $3k/year SME tier sold via newsletter, and a data feed to compliance-software vendors at $30-100k.
non_obvious_insight: Compliance is an options problem, not a deadline problem. Insiders sell obligations as fixed; the value is pricing probability and timing and finding multi-regime no-regret work. A public forecast track record is a moat law firms will not build because they cannot afford to be visibly wrong.
first_30_days: Publish a free 'Slip Index' showing the base rate of deadline moves across the 30 largest EU and US digital rules since 2023. Build a 500-person newsletter via IAPP-style and LinkedIn communities, and pre-sell 10 annual subscriptions at a $6k founder price with a money-back guarantee. Make every forecast in writing with a date.

title: Persistent Methane Plumes as Equipment Sales Leads
one_liner: Sell satellite-detected methane emitters to the vendors who profit from fixing them: a lead-gen engine, not a compliance tool.
customer: Vapor-recovery-unit makers, flare-gas-to-power microturbine and genset vendors, landfill gas-collection contractors, dairy digester and RNG developers, and small gas gatherers or offtakers. Roughly 2,000 companies in the US; first buyers are sales VPs at 20-person equipment firms.
problem: Abatement vendors prospect blind at trade shows. Emitters are often unaware of a persistent leak or vent, or they do not know its dollar value. A 500 kg/h plume is roughly 230,000 MMBtu a year, or about $0.7M of saleable gas at $3/MMBtu. Methane data today is sold to regulators, ESG buyers and the emitters themselves, and none of them are motivated.
solution: A weekly ranked lead list of persistent emitters, defined as repeated detections across passes from open Carbon Mapper, EMIT and Tanager plume products, with GHGSat tasking to confirm the best leads. Each lead joins the plume to facility ownership (state permits, landfill and EPA datasets), wasted-gas value per year, distance to pipeline or grid, and likely fix type. Delivered as a CRM feed plus a one-page dossier.
why_now: Plume data is now abundant and partly free: Carbon Mapper's Tanager publishes public plume products, and GHGSat is expanding to 16+ satellites. With US federal methane-penalty pressure pushed out, pitches built on fines are weak, while pitches built on recovering saleable gas still work. Cheap gas-to-power gensets and microturbines are also more available.
revenue_model: $2k to $6k a month per vendor per basin or vertical. Success fee of 2% to 4% of first-year equipment or service revenue on closed leads, capped. Later, sell offtake and RNG-interconnect leads to gas buyers.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone treats a methane plume as a violation to be reported. It is really an unmonetized commodity with a known street address and a quantifiable price. Selling the plume to the person who profits from fixing it inverts the market and does not depend on regulation.
first_30_days: Pull open plume data for the Permian, Appalachia and Ohio/Pennsylvania landfills and build the top 100 persistent emitters. Hand-verify ownership and gas value on each. Cold-offer 25 equipment vendors and landfill gas contractors three free leads, then $3k a month. Ask for a paid pilot from 3 by day 30.

title: Air-Permit Unlock for Idle Data Center Diesel
one_liner: Turn the ~55 GW of idle data center backup generators into dispatchable capacity by solving the air-permit problem instead of the hardware problem.
customer: Colo and hyperscale operators in PJM (Northern Virginia, Ohio, Illinois) with 20-500 MW of backup gensets. Secondary buyers are utilities and capacity buyers who need fast MW.
problem: Data centers hold about 55 GW of backup diesel (Virginia alone has about 27 GW permitted), and it runs 10-30 minutes a month. PJM cleared 6.8 GW short and wants large loads to bring their own capacity or be curtailed. Air permits cap non-emergency run hours, so nobody can legally count these engines as capacity.
solution: Fixed-price 'permit-to-dispatch' packages. They cover a state-specific permit modification strategy (run-hour caps, synthetic-minor limits), engineering and financing for emissions retrofits on the subset of engines that need them, and paralleling/telemetry upgrades. Enrollment in PJM's on-site backup (IRAS-style) and demand-response programs comes with third-party measurement and verification. Runtime is capped at a few dozen to ~100 hours a year, dispatched only in system emergencies, with community disclosure built in.
why_now: PJM's July auction shortfall, the proposed backstop auction (15-year terms, $555/MW-day cap) and the curtailment-or-bring-capacity rule make backup generation valuable for the first time. Turbines are sold out until 2029-30, so this fleet is the only large block of capacity that exists today.
revenue_model: $40-150k fixed fee per site for permit and engineering work, plus 10-20% of the first five years of capacity revenue. At the $325/MW-day cap a 20 MW fleet is worth very roughly $1.5-2M a year after derating, so the fee is easy to justify. Retrofit financing adds a spread.
non_obvious_insight: The cheapest big block of new PJM capacity is not new. It is already built and sitting behind a fence, and the barrier is air-permit lawyering that VC-backed hardware companies ignore. A repeatable per-state permit playbook is the moat. Emergency-only runtime is why it works: at under 1% of hours, the capacity value dwarfs the emissions.
first_30_days: Pull public Title V and minor-source permit files for ~30 colo sites in VA, OH and IL. Build a 'permit headroom map' showing run-hour caps and engine tiers. Retain one air-permitting consultant. Offer 25 facility and sustainability leads a $15k fixed-fee dispatch-readiness audit of a 20+ MW fleet and aim to close two paid pilots.

title: Warm-Backup Servicer for Orphaned Solar
one_liner: Be the standby operations-and-maintenance contractor for lenders and securitization trustees holding portfolios of systems whose installer died.
customer: Trustees and servicers of solar loan and lease securitizations, tax-equity and debt holders, and buyers of distressed portfolios. Homeowners can buy direct as a secondary channel.
problem: Sunnova, Titan, ADT Solar and Freedom Forever failed. Manufacturer warranties survive but nobody supplies the service labor, and monitoring clouds die. Customers with dead inverters stop paying, which erodes the cash flows lenders depend on.
solution: A backup-servicing contract. Onboard the portfolio's asset data, replace dead monitoring clouds with a local gateway, dispatch vetted local technicians through a roll-up network, handle manufacturer RMA and warranty claims, and upsell battery retrofit and VPP enrollment.
why_now: The bankruptcy wave of 2024-26 has portfolios sitting in trustees' hands. With 25D gone there are fewer new installers. A 46% storage attach rate means more complex systems in the field.
revenue_model: $8-15 per system-month standby retainer, a $250-450 margin per truck roll, an RMA handling fee, and referral fees for battery and VPP enrollments.
non_obvious_insight: Lenders do not care about kilowatts. They care about payments, and a homeowner with a dead inverter stops paying. Service is a credit-protection product, and its buyer is the party with the balance sheet and the pain.
first_30_days: Identify three distressed portfolios from trustee reports and call the servicers. Sign a 1,000-system pilot in one metro. Onboard two local service shops. Build the gateway on vendor APIs and local Modbus.

title: Jobs-per-Megawatt Factory Recruiting for Public Power
one_liner: Represent municipal electric utilities in recruiting manufacturers by packaging spare feeder capacity, in-hand transformers and industrial rates into a 'jobs per megawatt' pitch that data centers cannot match.
customer: Municipal and public-power utilities and city economic-development agencies (retainer of roughly $3-6k a month). Manufacturers pay a success fee later.
problem: Data centers are absorbing grid capacity, and transformer and switchgear prices are up 89-96% since 2019. Factory construction is down 22-32% from peak while nondefense capital-goods orders hit a record $85.9B, so reshoring is happening as retrofits that need power upgrades, not as new shells. Interconnection at investor-owned utilities takes years, and site selectors rarely look at small public utilities.
solution: A 'Load-Readiness Dossier' per feeder or substation: available megawatts, transformer status and lead times, industrial rate schedules, demand-charge modeling and permitting path. Match it to manufacturers with announced expansions (tariff-motivated onshoring, USMCA re-routers, foundries and magnet or metal processors) and to site selectors. Add a shared transformer reserve pool for small municipal utilities and help negotiate long-term service commitments.
why_now: Data-center demand collided with the reshoring wave in 2026. Section 232 tiers reward US-melted metals and full-value duties are pushing firms to add domestic capacity, and the machinery tier's 15% relief runs through 2027. Utilities are being asked to make loads decisions faster than most can handle.
revenue_model: $3-6k a month retainer per utility, a success fee per megawatt or per signed customer (paid by the manufacturer or shared), and optional financing of pre-bought transformer inventory.
non_obvious_insight: A public utility's incentives are the reverse of an investor-owned utility's. A 5 MW machining plant with hundreds of jobs beats a 100 MW data center with a few dozen jobs for a city council and for spreading fixed costs, yet no one markets to these utilities. Transformer-in-hand is the strongest closing argument.
first_30_days: Select 10 public-power utilities in manufacturing states (Ohio, Indiana, Tennessee, Texas, the Carolinas) and build dossiers from public tariffs, EIA data and integrated resource plans. Pitch 3 economic-development agencies and sign two paid pilot retainers.

title: Paid Holds: Options Market for Booking Agents
one_liner: A merchant plugin that sells time-limited holds on appointments, tables and inventory to shopping and booking agents, so agent traffic becomes fee revenue for the merchant instead of something to block.
customer: Wallet-holding consumer assistant agents and browser agents, which pay through AP2, ACP or Stripe/Tempo MPP rails. Supply side is independent restaurants, salons, dentists, physios, tee-time, boat and experience operators on Acuity, Square Appointments, Booksy, Cal.com or Mindbody.
problem: Agents shop in parallel. One errand fans out to 20-50 merchants and the agent wants to keep the best option open until its principal approves. Free holds are free options, so merchants see phantom demand, no-show slots and sold-out tables. Their response is to block agents: eBay barred buy-for-me agents in Feb 2026 and Amazon blocked Meta's Muse agent on 22 Sept 2026.
solution: The merchant sets a hold price (for example 2-5% of ticket value, $1 minimum) and a duration (10 minutes to 24 hours). The agent calls hold(), pays programmatically and gets a signed hold receipt the merchant honors. If the agent converts, the fee is credited to the booking. If not, the merchant keeps it and we take 25%. The service also dedupes so retrying agents don't double-book. Later, hold prices float with demand, giving each slot an implied option value.
why_now: Google's AP2 v0.2 added human-not-present payments and moved to the FIDO Alliance. Stripe and Tempo's Machine Payments Protocol went live in March 2026, and Visa and Mastercard both have agent rails. Merchants are blocking agents right now, and the Ninth Circuit vacated Amazon's injunction against Perplexity in Aug 2026, so blocking is legally shaky. Visa expects millions of agent-made purchases this holiday season.
revenue_model: 25% of hold fees, plus a 1-2% referral fee on converted bookings. The merchant plugin is free to install. Later, a paid demand-analytics dashboard for merchants showing agent search intent by slot.
non_obvious_insight: Merchants are not hostile to agents. They are hostile to free options. Agents are the first buyers rational enough to price optionality, so charging for holds turns an adversarial scraping problem into a market. Airlines already sell fare holds, so the concept is proven with humans. Agents make it viable at $1 scale, and the hold price becomes a demand signal merchants have never had.
first_30_days: Build on the public webhooks and APIs of Cal.com, Acuity and Square Appointments. Recruit about 40 independent salons, barbers and physios in one metro with a free plugin, paying them out of our own test agents' wallets. Ship an MCP server exposing hold_and_book. Get 3 consumer-agent or browser-agent builders to integrate through x402/MPP hackathons. Measure hold-to-book conversion and no-show reduction, then charge live fees in months 2-3.

title: Driver's Ed for Smartphones, Sold to Parent Groups
one_liner: Ten-week, cohort-based 'phone license' programs where a whole grade's parents and kids pledge together, kids earn tiered device access through in-person challenges, and the finish is a coming-of-age ceremony.
customer: Parent groups for one grade at one school (PTA/PTO, church youth groups, scout troops, neighborhoods) with kids aged 9-13 facing the first-smartphone decision. Parents pay about $249 per child. PTAs get a rev-share. Later: device partners and employers offering parent benefits.
problem: The first smartphone is a collective-action problem ('everyone else has one'). Parental-control software fails technically (7 in 10 Australian under-16s reportedly still hold accounts) and socially. The first phone has become an unguided adolescent initiation with no ritual, no community and no meaning, while loneliness among the young is rising.
solution: 1) A Parent Pact night to agree shared rules. 2) Ten weekly 90-minute kid sessions with trained youth facilitators covering boredom, friendship, spotting manipulative design, AI-companion literacy and group-chat etiquette, with badges earned in person. 3) Tiered device 'licenses': none, then dumbphone or watch, then a filtered smartphone using OS-level age signals, then full access, each unlocked at cohort milestones with parent sign-off. 4) A License Ceremony with families. 5) An alumni circle with monthly meetups and a parent forum.
why_now: Under-16 bans (Australia Dec 2025, Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Florida) and app-store or OS-level age-assurance laws (California's Digital Age Assurance Act, Texas) are tiering the internet by age. Roblox now tiers by age (Kids, Select, standard). Support for Australia's ban has fallen to 57% and enforcement is leaky, so parents need a home-side complement. Twelve US states have school phone bans.
revenue_model: About $249 per child per cohort, a 15% rev-share to PTAs, bounties on tier-appropriate device or plan activations (verify what partners will pay), a $600 facilitator certification for teachers and youth workers, and later employer-paid parent benefits.
non_obvious_insight: The first smartphone fails as a family decision but works as a class decision. Because the product synchronizes a social graph, its moat is the cohort, not code. And a secular rite of passage supplies the 'meaning' that makes kids willing, which content-filtering apps cannot provide.
first_30_days: Pilot with two elementary schools' 4th- and 5th-grade parent groups through PTA presidents and 'Wait Until 8th' pledge lists. Recruit four facilitators (education or psychology students and retired coaches). Charge $249, run cohorts October-December so graduation lands before holiday phone gifting, and track how many kids stay phone-free until 13.

title: PFAS Farm Passport for Food Buyers and Lenders
one_liner: A screening-plus-sampling service that tells dairy co-ops, produce processors and ag lenders which supplier farms carry PFAS risk from sludge spreading or contaminated irrigation water, and certifies the clean ones.
customer: Dairy co-ops, regional produce and hay buyers, private-label sourcing teams and agricultural lenders. The buyer pays for its supplier base, and farms pay for re-verification.
problem: The industry frames PFAS as a 4 ppt tap-water rule, and EPA's proposed delay to 2031 and rescissions seem to give slack. The abrupt financial shock is on farms: biosolids-spread fields and PFAS-laden irrigation or well water (Maine's shut-down farms are the precedent). There is no farm-level limit, so lenders and buyers cannot underwrite.
solution: A 'PFAS Farm Passport'. First, a desktop risk screen from public biosolids-application permits, industrial discharger locations and nearby well data. Second, a targeted sampling protocol (irrigation water, soil, forage, milk) run through a partner lab. Third, a risk tier and a 'verified clean' attestation for buyers and lenders. Fourth, remediation triage (change water source, crop or field use).
why_now: Regulatory loosening pushes risk assessment onto private buyers, who cannot wait for rules. The 2027 monitoring data will make PFAS geography public. Maine-style farm closures have put buyers on notice, and private supplier standards tend to outrun public ones.
revenue_model: $300-800 desktop screen per farm (paid by buyer), $1-3k per sampling round, $100-300k/yr enterprise contracts for processors with 500-2,000 suppliers, and lender portfolio-screening fees.
non_obvious_insight: Buyers fear being caught selling contaminated milk, not violating a tap-water limit. In food supply chains a private standard beats the public rule, so the gap between the EPA rollback and buyer fear is the market.
first_30_days: Choose one region with open biosolids-application records (Michigan, Wisconsin or Maine). Screen 500 farms desktop-only. Give three regional dairy co-ops or processors a free 'top 20 at-risk suppliers' preview, and sell a paid 50-farm sampling pilot.

title: Pet Sitters as Home-Energy Field Workforce
one_liner: A trained, insured network of pet sitters and dog walkers who already hold house keys and midday access, performing unlicensed home-energy tasks that stall electrification programs.
customer: VPP and DR aggregators, utility weatherization and heat pump programs, and home-battery/heat-pump installers that pay per completed visit ($40-90). Homeowners see it as free or discounted enrollment.
problem: Electricians are scarce (about 81,000 openings a year) and data centers pay 25-30% premiums, so home electrification loses labor. But many program stalls are not licensed work: 'customer must be home' no-shows, devices offline, thermostat and smart-plug swaps, filter changes, weatherstripping, photos for interconnection paperwork, and plug-in solar setup. Each one is a truck roll priced like an electrician's.
solution: Recruit and background-check pet sitters and walkers, insure them, and train them on about a dozen no-license tasks with guided QR workflows. Schedule tasks alongside pet visits, with the owner's explicit opt-in and strict limits (plug-in and low-voltage only, no panel work). Route orders from utilities, VPP operators and installers, and include placement of pet-zone sensors where relevant.
why_now: Data-center wage arbitrage is draining electricians (one report shows $20 to $35 an hour), 25C/25D subsidies ended so programs are cutting cost per home, and at least nine states have signed plug-in solar laws (around 1.2 kW, UL 3700 exists), which makes non-electrician installs legal and needed.
revenue_model: Per-visit fee billed to the program ($40-90) with 25-35% margin after sitter pay, training and certification fees, and a subscription for large programs that need a managed scheduling and QA layer.
non_obvious_insight: The energy transition's shortage is not just electricians. A large slice of tasks need access and trust rather than a license, and pet sitters uniquely hold both, visit on a schedule, and are a labor pool data centers cannot poach.
first_30_days: Pick one metro where a local sitter collective or Rover/Wag-heavy sitter community exists. Recruit and train 20 sitters on 5 tasks (thermostat, smart plug, offline-device reconnect, filter swap, plug-in solar setup). Sell a pilot at $60/visit to one co-op or heat-pump installer needing post-install commissioning and connectivity fixes. Confirm liability coverage before the first visit.

title: Prize-Money Payout and Tax Withholding for Sports Tours
one_liner: A payout engine for pro-am tours and event organizers that KYCs athletes, collects tax forms, withholds correctly on nonresident winners, files the paperwork, and pays in local currency or stablecoin within 24 hours instead of on a 60-day wire.
customer: Organizers of tours and one-off events with international fields and $50k-$5M purses: pickleball, padel, fitness racing such as Hyrox, BJJ and grappling, trail ultras, surf and CrossFit-style competitions. Agents and athlete associations are secondary users.
problem: US-source prize money paid to nonresident athletes is generally subject to 30% withholding unless treaty status is properly documented, with W-8 forms and 1042-S filings. Small organizers mishandle this and carry penalty risk. Athletes wait weeks for wires that cost $25-45 plus FX spread. Athletes in countries like Kenya or Ethiopia often lose another 10-20% to agents, and payments to unbanked winners are a mess.
solution: A payee vault that holds W-8 and W-9 forms, treaty article claims and sanctions screening. The organizer funds the purse by ACH. The engine applies split rules for sponsor, agent, team and coach, calculates withholding by treaty and state, files 1042-S and 1099 forms, and pays out to bank accounts, mobile money or USDC wallets through partners in supported corridors. Payouts can be triggered at the podium. Each payout also creates a verified earnings record for the athlete.
why_now: Independent tours and pro-am leagues have multiplied and raised purses through 2024-26. Stablecoins are now regulated plumbing after the GENIUS Act, with the Fed proposing issuer rules on Sept 24, 2026. Circle's $400M Tazapay deal and Yellow Card's $40M raise are building local payout rails in emerging markets. The 1% US remittance tax on cash-funded transfers pushes senders toward digital rails.
revenue_model: 1.0-1.5% of purse volume, $15-25 per payee onboarding, $10 per 1042-S filed, and an FX spread. A tour paying out $10M a year yields about $150k in revenue.
non_obvious_insight: Sports' payout problem is not moving money, it is proving who is owed what and what to withhold. The rail is a commodity while the compliance file is the moat. Every payout also produces an athlete-verified earnings record, which lets a semi-pro athlete prove income for a bank, visa or insurer, something thin-margin athletes cannot do today.
first_30_days: Pick two fragmented sports with foreign fields, such as a trail-ultra series and a mid-tier pickleball or padel tour. Offer to run payouts for one event at cost. Use a fractional international-tax CPA plus Stripe Connect, Wise or Airwallex for the plumbing. Pre-build a treaty table for the top 30 athlete home countries. Charge 1.5% from the second event onward and aim for five events in 90 days.

title: Bring-Into-Use Satellites for Spectrum Filing Holders
one_liner: Fixed-price rideshare satellites that let holders of valuable spectrum and orbit filings meet ITU hardware milestones instead of losing them.
customer: Telecom ministries and regulators of small and mid-size states (Gulf, Africa, Pacific, Central Asia, Latin America), plus startups that hold NGSO filings but cannot afford a full constellation.
problem: Spectrum and orbit rights are now priced like beachfront (EchoStar's reported $23B sale to AT&T and $17B sale to SpaceX), yet ITU rules still require real hardware in orbit by set deadlines. A holder of paper filings is one missed milestone from losing the asset, and a real constellation costs hundreds of millions.
solution: A standard 6U-12U bus with a software-defined payload configurable to the filed bands, sold as a 'milestone in a box'. The package covers rideshare launch, operations, evidence for the administration and coordination paperwork. Regulatory counsel decides what counts as bringing into use for each filing. Entry product is a filing-health audit built from public ITU data.
why_now: The 2025-26 EchoStar deals reset what spectrum is worth. Rideshare is plentiful (321 orbital launches in 2025 per the briefing). Commercial 6U buses and SDR payloads are off the shelf, and nine-figure rounds at European bus makers show integration capacity is growing. Sovereign space programs are multiplying.
revenue_model: Audit $20-50k. Fixed-price milestone satellite $1.5-4M. Annual retainer of $100-300k for filing maintenance and coordination. Optional success fee when a preserved filing is sold or leased.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders treat filings as paper assets and hardware as optional. The ITU makes hardware the price of keeping the paper, so the scarce thing is cheap, compliant placeholder hardware plus the regulatory playbook. Nobody sells that as a product.
first_30_days: Hire one ex-administration or ITU filing specialist on contract. Scrape public ITU filing data and rank about 100 filings by deadline urgency. Send personalized audits to 50 administrations and startups, and charge for the first five. Collect LOI-backed pre-orders before committing to hardware.

title: GLP-1 Alcohol Protocols Inside Sober-Living Homes
one_liner: A turnkey semaglutide-for-alcohol-use-disorder protocol delivered through recovery residences, which supply the daily accountability, testing and peer community that telehealth prescribing lacks.
customer: Sober-living and recovery-residence operators and intensive-outpatient centers, who pass the cost into resident fees of $600-2,500 a month that are usually paid by families.
problem: Very few people with alcohol use disorder get any medication, and a Lancet RCT (May 2026, n=108) showed semaglutide cut heavy drinking days with an NNT of 4.3 versus 7+ for approved drugs. GLP-1 prescribing for it is off-label and sold as DTC telehealth to isolated individuals. Recovery houses have residents, house managers and drug testing, but no medical capability. Operators bleed occupancy and reputation on relapse evictions, and GLP-1 use in liver-compromised drinkers carries real malnutrition, muscle-loss and GI risks that need monitoring.
solution: A partner addiction-medicine physician or telehealth prescriber panel screens and consents residents, using contraindication checks and baseline labs. House managers get training and a daily check-in script (dose day, intake, nausea, cravings). A dietitian sets minimum protein and calorie floors. Weekly peer-recovery groups link medication, craving and community, with a tapering and aftercare plan at discharge. The house sees 30/60/90-day retention and abstinence data.
why_now: The 2026 Lancet RCT and $149-299 cash prices for branded GLP-1s make the drug affordable. Compounded supply is closing, which pushes demand toward branded, clinician-supervised use. Many states are certifying recovery residences, and Medicaid cuts in 2027 make private-pay operators look for outcomes-based differentiation.
revenue_model: $120-200 per resident per month from operators (passed through in rent), plus clinician-visit billing or revenue share with the prescriber, and an aftercare subscription for graduates.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input for alcohol-use-disorder pharmacotherapy is adherence and monitoring, not the prescription. Telehealth sells scripts to lonely individuals, while sober-living houses already have people living together with daily check-ins and testing. The house is the missing delivery infrastructure, and GLP-1 gives it the first credible craving-reduction drug to offer.
first_30_days: Sign one addiction-medicine physician and three operators in one metro (Florida, Texas or California). Enroll about 20 consenting residents with written informed consent, and track 30/60/90-day retention and abstinence days versus the houses' baselines. Use the data to sign the next 10 houses. Get a healthcare attorney's review of the off-label and consent framework before the first dose.

title: Outside-Processing Milk Run for Job Shops
one_liner: Scheduled pickup routes and batching software for the heat-treat, plating and anodize bottleneck behind reshored machining.
customer: 10-100 person machine shops and fabricators, plus special-process houses (heat treat, anodize, plating, passivation, paint) that want fuller batches.
problem: As machining orders rise (machinery jobs +6.1k in August, record capital-goods orders), the constraint moves downstream to special processes. Shops ship parts by carrier ad hoc, parts sit in queues, and paperwork gets lost. ISM supplier deliveries have slowed for eight straight months. Environmental cost and owner retirements limit new special-process capacity (my inference).
solution: Vans on fixed weekly or daily routes between shops and vetted process vendors. Batching gives vendors full loads. Barcode chain of custody carries cert paperwork (heat-treat charts, NADCAP status). A promised turnaround (for example 5 days) is tracked by software.
why_now: Reshoring in existing walls raises job counts while outside-process capacity has not grown. Slowing deliveries make lead time visible.
revenue_model: Per-stop fee plus 8-12% margin on outside-processing volume. Vendor SaaS. Later, acquire a heat-treat or anodize house.
non_obvious_insight: Outside processing often accounts for most of a job's elapsed lead time but only a small share of touch time. That bottleneck yields to logistics and batching, not new furnaces, and adding a van is cheaper than adding an oven.
first_30_days: Pick one region such as Grand Rapids, Greenville or Wichita. Interview 20 shops. Sign two heat-treat or anodize houses. Run a one-van pilot two days a week and charge per stop.

title: Disaster-Pause Rider for Small-Business Loans
one_liner: A parametric portfolio rider that lets CDFIs and credit unions automatically pause small-business and farm loan payments after a disaster, with the lender made whole by a pre-funded payout.
customer: Community lenders (CDFIs, credit unions, farm-credit and small-bank lenders) with $50-$500M loan books in disaster-exposed counties. The end beneficiaries are their small-business and consumer borrowers.
problem: After a hurricane, flood or fire, borrowers need a payment holiday, but lenders cannot afford to grant them automatically because the missed cash flow strains liquidity and reserves. Borrowers must plead, forbearance takes weeks of staff time, and many quietly default. CDFI funding is already fragile, so lenders hold back.
solution: A portfolio-level parametric policy keyed to county-level disaster declarations plus hazard footprints (wind swaths, flood extent, fire perimeters). It pays the lender the scheduled payments of borrowers in the footprint for 90-180 days. The loan documents carry a pre-approved 'automatic pause' clause, so borrowers never buy insurance. The lender markets 'storm-proof loans' and adds a rate rider of about 10-25 bps to pay for it. A software pause engine flags affected loans and sends notices.
why_now: Repeated large disasters and ongoing debate over shrinking or slowing federal disaster aid make private, fast liquidity more attractive. Federal support for CDFIs has been unsettled, so lenders want to protect portfolios. Parametric capacity is abundant and hazard-footprint data (NOAA swaths, flood extents) is public and precise.
revenue_model: MGA/brokerage fee of 15-20% on premium (roughly 25-60 bps of covered balance per year), plus a SaaS fee of $1,000-$5,000 per month for the pause-and-notice engine. Later, reinsurance placement and a data product on borrower resilience.
non_obvious_insight: After a disaster the scarce resource is lender liquidity, not rebuilding capital. A forbearance favor becomes a contractual right that costs the lender one clause, and distribution is the loan itself, so no borrower ever has to shop for or understand insurance.
first_30_days: Approach three Gulf Coast, Carolinas or California CDFIs and credit unions through CDFI trade networks. Write a one-page term sheet, price it from historical hazard footprints, and pilot on newly originated loans in one county. Pair with an MGA and a reinsurer, and target one signed letter of intent within 60 days.

title: Archival Footage Authenticity Clearance for Documentaries
one_liner: A per-film clearance service that proves each archival still and clip is real, so producers and E&O insurers can sign off.
customer: Independent documentary producers, YouTube documentary channels and news video teams, plus clearance consultants and E&O brokers that refer them.
problem: Clearance houses check rights, not reality. Stock libraries and search results now contain AI-made 'archival' images, and one fake in a true-crime doc becomes a public scandal, as with the AI images alleged in Netflix's What Jennifer Did (2024). E&O underwriters ask for clearance procedures. Visible AI watermarks are unreliable, since removers for Sora output appeared within a week of its launch.
solution: Fixed-price audit of a film's cut list. For each asset: trace it to the earliest source via reverse search and archive catalogs, run metadata and codec forensics, check C2PA and SynthID where available, run a detector ensemble, and produce a provenance chain. Deliver a per-asset source dossier and a producer's memo formatted for insurers and distributors. A portal re-checks only assets that change between cuts.
why_now: Sora's shutdown (app Apr 26, API Sep 24) removes one source, but open video models keep flooding stock sources. Streamers publish AI guidelines, and TikTok's C2PA membership in Jul 2026 normalizes provenance checks.
revenue_model: $1.5-10k per film, $500-3k/month for YouTube documentary or news teams, and referral fees from clearance consultants.
non_obvious_insight: Rights clearance is already a budgeted line item in every documentary. Authenticity clearance is a new column in an existing spreadsheet, so it does not need a new budget line.
first_30_days: Reach five documentary producers via the International Documentary Association and doc-maker Slack groups. Run a free audit on one recently published film's archival section, partner with two clearance consultants for referrals, and charge $2.5k for the next five.

title: Ear-Coach for Early-Ed Teachers, Paid by QRIS
one_liner: Classroom-audio analysis that scores teacher-child interactions the way trained CLASS observers do and coaches staff weekly, sold to centers as a path to higher state quality-rating tiers and higher reimbursement.
customer: Directors and owners of centers and small chains (5-50 sites) in states with tiered-reimbursement QRIS programs. Also QRIS coaching contractors and Head Start grantees.
problem: Insiders picture AI in early education as child-facing. The real bottleneck is the adult: the average worker earns $33,140, turnover is high and coaching is sporadic. Quality-rating tiers drive subsidy-rate bonuses, but observation-based scoring needs scarce, costly trained observers, so centers stay stuck at low stars.
solution: Opt-in classroom audio pods or teacher-worn mics with on-device diarization and transcription (no child audio retained). They score serve-and-return turns, open-ended questions, language richness and tone. Each teacher gets a 3-minute weekly micro-coaching note on their phone, and directors get a mock-CLASS 'star readiness' report before official visits.
why_now: On-device diarization and transcription are cheap and good enough. New tax credits and subsidy money (45F at 40-50%, DCFSA to $7,500) are landing in centers in 2026. Child-facing AI is drawing lawsuits, while teacher-facing AI avoids that liability.
revenue_model: $40-80 per classroom per month, plus an optional success fee (a share of the reimbursement uplift) when the center's tier rises.
non_obvious_insight: Quality is a lever on price, since higher-tier centers earn higher reimbursement, so coaching can be sold as revenue rather than a cost. Putting AI in the adult's ear sidesteps the child-AI liability wave entirely.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 centers in a state that pays tier bonuses. Record consented lessons on phones and run open-source diarization. Have two ex-CLASS observers score 20 clips to validate the model's ratings. Sell a $500 'star readiness audit' per center, then convert to a monthly plan.
